lab_title: Cardiac Anatomy and Blood Flow: The Human Heart and Pulmonary-Systemic Circulation
top_level_objectives: Identify the four chambers of the heart and explain their structural differences
Locate and name the four valves and explain their directional function
Trace the path of blood through both pulmonary and systemic circulation loops
Understand why the left ventricle has thicker myocardium than the right ventricle
Recognize major blood vessels entering and leaving the heart and their functions

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the gross anatomy of the heart and locate the four chambers in anatomical position. Students see an interactive 3D model of the heart from anterior and lateral views, with chambers labeled and color-coded by oxygenation status (deoxygenated chambers in darker blue, oxygenated in red).
key_visuals: 3D anatomical model of the intact heart in anterior view
Color-coded chambers: deoxygenated (right atrium and right ventricle in darker blue), oxygenated (left atrium and left ventricle in red)
Labels pointing to: right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, left ventricle
Transparent overlay showing chamber walls and relative wall thickness
student_actions: Tap on each chamber to reveal its name and basic function
Rotate the model to view chambers from multiple angles (anterior, lateral, posterior)
Compare the visual thickness of the left vs. right ventricular walls and note the difference
Identify which chambers contain oxygenated vs. deoxygenated blood in the static heart model

scenes.brief_purpose: Examine the structure and placement of the four valves. The heart is shown in frontal section with each valve highlighted individually. Students learn valve location, the chambers it separates, and its valve leaflets/cusps.
key_visuals: Frontal cross-section of the heart exposing all four valve locations
Each valve highlighted in sequence: tricuspid (between right atrium and right ventricle, shown with three cusps)
Pulmonary valve (at the exit of right ventricle into pulmonary trunk, shown with three cusps)
Mitral/bicuspid valve (between left atrium and left ventricle, shown with two cusps)
Aortic valve (at the exit of left ventricle into aorta, shown with three cusps)
Labels and anatomical annotations for each valve
student_actions: Tap each valve in sequence to highlight it and hear its name and location
Count the cusps/leaflets on each valve and note structural differences
Identify which chambers each valve separates
Determine the direction blood normally flows through each valve
Discuss why valves are one-directional (prevent backflow)

scenes.scene_name: Major Blood Vessels: Entry and Exit
scenes.brief_purpose: Visualize the major vessels connected to the heart. The model shows the heart with vessels labeled in their anatomical positions: superior vena cava, inferior vena cava, pulmonary arteries (right and left), pulmonary veins, and aorta. Color coding (blue for deoxygenated, red for oxygenated) helps distinguish vessel content.
key_visuals: 3D heart model with major vessels attached and extending outward
Superior vena cava (blue) entering right atrium from above
Inferior vena cava (blue) entering right atrium from below
Pulmonary trunk dividing into right and left pulmonary arteries (blue, leaving right ventricle)
Right and left pulmonary veins (red, returning to left atrium)
Aorta (red, exiting left ventricle upward and curving)
Color-coded labels and brief text descriptions of each vessel's origin and destination
student_actions: Tap on each vessel to hear its name, chamber connection, and functional role
Trace the blue (deoxygenated) vessels and note they bring blood TO the heart
Trace the red (oxygenated) vessels and note they bring blood FROM the lungs and TO the body
Identify which vessels are arteries vs. veins based on direction of blood flow
Predict which part of the body each vessel connects to

scenes.brief_purpose: Animate the path of deoxygenated blood through the right side of the heart and lungs. A glowing particle flow shows blood entering the right atrium via the venae cavae, passing through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, being pumped through the pulmonary valve and pulmonary arteries to the lungs.
key_visuals: 3D heart model with lungs shown in anatomical position on either side
Animated blue particle flow starting from the venae cavae entering the right atrium
Flow passes through tricuspid valve (highlighted in green when open) into right ventricle
Right ventricle contracts (visual wall movement) pumping blood through pulmonary valve into pulmonary arteries
Particles travel along pulmonary arteries to the lung tissue
Text annotations marking each stage: "Deoxygenated blood returns from body," "Right atrium fills," "Tricuspid valve opens," etc.
Numbered steps (1-4) guiding the sequence
student_actions: Watch the animation and follow the blue blood particles from body to lungs
Pause the animation at each major step and identify the chamber or valve involved
Tap on the tricuspid valve and pulmonary valve when highlighted to understand their opening
Explain why the right ventricle's wall is thinner (only needs to pump to nearby lungs)
Answer: What is the purpose of the pulmonary circulation?

scenes.brief_purpose: Animate the path of oxygenated blood through the left side of the heart to the systemic circulation. A glowing particle flow shows blood returning from the lungs via the pulmonary veins into the left atrium, passing through the mitral valve into the left ventricle, and being pumped through the aortic valve into the aorta for distribution to the entire body.
key_visuals: 3D heart model with schematic representation of the systemic circulation (body outline or simplified organ systems)
Animated red particle flow starting from pulmonary veins entering the left atrium
Flow passes through mitral valve (highlighted in green when open) into left ventricle
Left ventricle contracts (visual wall movement more pronounced than right) pumping blood through aortic valve into the aorta
Particles travel along the aorta and branch to represent systemic distribution
Text annotations marking each stage: "Oxygenated blood from lungs," "Left atrium fills," "Mitral valve opens," etc.
Numbered steps (5-8) continuing the sequence from the pulmonary loop
student_actions: Watch the animation and follow the red blood particles from lungs through the left heart to the body
Pause the animation at each major step and identify the chamber or valve involved
Tap on the mitral valve and aortic valve when highlighted to understand their opening
Compare the thickness and contraction force of the left ventricle to the right (observed visually)
Explain: Why does the left ventricle need a thicker myocardium? (Systemic circulation requires more force)

scenes.scene_name: Complete Cardiac Cycle and Dual-Loop Integration
scenes.brief_purpose: Show the complete path of blood through both pulmonary and systemic circulation in one continuous animation. This integrates all previous learning: deoxygenated blood loops through the lungs and oxygenated blood loops through the body, both driven by the contracting heart chambers.
key_visuals: Full 3D anatomical view showing the heart, lungs, and simplified representation of systemic circulation
Dual-color particle system: blue particles tracing the pulmonary loop simultaneously with red particles tracing the systemic loop
All four chambers and four valves visible with color-coded highlighting during their respective phases
Timeline or cycle indicator showing position in the cardiac cycle (atrial systole → ventricular systole → diastole)
Summary labels: "Right side pumps to lungs (pulmonary circulation)," "Left side pumps to body (systemic circulation)"
student_actions: Watch the complete dual-loop animation showing both circuits operating simultaneously
Identify the timing: when right ventricle pumps, left ventricle also pumps (simultaneous contraction)
Trace both loops independently by focusing on blue vs. red particles
Pause at key moments (atrial fill, ventricular contraction, valve opening/closing) and identify what's happening
Explain how the heart is actually two pumps working in series (right then left) but appearing simultaneous due to cardiac cycle timing

scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate how valves prevent backflow during the cardiac cycle. The animation shows each valve opening and closing in context, with a visual explanation of what happens if a valve fails (illustrative only—showing regurgitation/backflow as a burst of reverse-flowing particles).
key_visuals: Zoomed 3D views of each valve during its functional phase
Tricuspid valve: opens when right atrium contracts, closes when right ventricle contracts (shows valve cusps moving)
Pulmonary valve: opens when right ventricle contracts, closes immediately after (prevents backflow into ventricle)
Mitral valve: opens when left atrium contracts, closes when left ventricle contracts
Aortic valve: opens when left ventricle contracts, closes immediately after (prevents backflow from aorta)
For each valve, an inset showing the consequence of failure: reverse flow (backflow) represented by reversed particle motion or leak animation
student_actions: Observe each valve opening and closing through one complete cycle
For each valve, identify when it opens (pressure gradient favoring forward flow) and closes (pressure reversal)
Tap on a valve to see what happens if it becomes incompetent (leaky) or stenotic (too narrow)
Explain in their own words: How does the pressure gradient determine valve direction?
Discuss the clinical relevance: What happens in valve disease (e.g., murmurs from regurgitation)?

scenes.scene_name: Myocardial Thickness Comparison and Functional Significance
scenes.brief_purpose: Directly compare the wall thickness of the left and right ventricles and explain the structural-functional relationship. Side-by-side cross-sections show the difference in myocardial mass, with annotations explaining that the left ventricle must generate higher pressure to pump blood throughout the entire body.
key_visuals: Side-by-side longitudinal cross-sections: right ventricle on left, left ventricle on right
Clear visual contrast: right ventricular wall visibly thinner, left ventricular wall visibly thicker
Measurements or scale labels showing approximate wall thickness ratio (left wall ~3x thicker than right)
Overlay showing the internal chamber volumes (similar size) vs. wall mass (significantly different)
Annotation boxes: "Right ventricle: pumps to lungs (~25 mmHg)," "Left ventricle: pumps to entire body (~120 mmHg systolic)"
student_actions: Visually compare the myocardial wall thickness between ventricles
Estimate or measure the wall thickness ratio using on-screen tools or reference guides
Explain why the left ventricle needs more muscular mass (higher workload, greater resistance in systemic circulation)
Relate this to the concept of Laplace's law and wall stress: a thicker wall develops greater pressure
Discuss: What would happen to the left ventricle over time if it had thin walls like the right ventricle? (Ventricular dilation, heart failure)
